faqs.q: Someone in our Port St. Lucie group posted an iguana photo — is the city infested?
faqs.a: No. Port St. Lucie is report-level iguana territory: scattered sightings, often near canals, tracked by FWC, without established breeding colonies of the South Florida kind. Photograph and report sightings; check your own seawall or canal bank for burrows; and if an individual animal takes up residence on your property, humane removal there is lawful — relocation never is. Citywide infestation claims are a sales tactic, and the honest local answer is vigilance without a program contract.

faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Fort Pierce?
faqs.a: Nine-banded armadillos dig for grubs and earthworms in lawns and flower beds, and they are common throughout most of Florida, including Fort Pierce. A live-trapped armadillo may be released on-site, or released within the same county on 40 or more contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission, within 24 hours — those are the Florida rules, and we follow them. We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.

Fort Pierce.wildlife_intro:
In Fort Pierce, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — fast-growing master-planned suburbs, older lagoon cities, and barrier-island communities — and features such as Indian River Lagoon, Savannas Preserve State Park, North Fork St. Lucie River, Hutchinson Island keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Fort Pierce jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: Roof rats come off the grove behind our Lakewood Park home — will sealing hold?
faqs.a: Yes — grove rats are commuters, and a sealed house ends the commute. Roof rats shelter in citrus and forage widely; the attic is their preferred den, entered at the roofline. The grove population stays — that is agriculture — but a closed house is closed, season after season, while unsealed neighbors keep hosting. That is the whole strategy, and it works.

faqs.q: Moles or armadillos — how do we know what is digging in Indian River Estates?
faqs.a: Read the yard at breakfast. An armadillo works at night and leaves many shallow, cone-shaped holes and pushed-up turf where it hunted grubs. An eastern mole leaves raised tunnels — soft ridges across the lawn — and small round hills. A single large half-moon burrow with a sand apron is a gopher tortoise, protected, and the diagnosis becomes a buffer. We sort it on inspection and only quote treatment for the animal that is actually digging.
